title: Even Baron, Rivet, Wendelin, Pareus, Maresius deny past-remission trust is the justifying act
source_text: CXXIV. Imo illi ipsi Scholae Reformatae Doctores, quorum testimonio praecipue nititur autor ille, qui corruptae Christi Ethices Reformatos accusat, ut toti eorum Scholae tribuat eam sententiam, quod actus fidei per quem justificamur, sit certa fiducia de obtenta a Deo peccatorum venia, expresse & diserte negant se istud sentire; ut abunde supra probatum est, allatis verbis & testimoniis Roberti Baronii, Riveti, Wendelini, Paraei, Maresii. Baronium nempe, distinguere inter fiduciam veniae impetrandae, & fiduciam veniae impetratae: utramque ipsi esse actum proprium fidei justificantis; sed priorem praecedere justificationem, & esse ejus instrumentum; posteriorem vero sequi justificationem, nec ejus instrumentum esse. Rivetum autem, Wendelinum, Paraeum, & Maresium subtilius adhuc distinguere inter fiduciam, qua credit aliquis peccata sibi remittenda, illam qua credit peccata sibi in praesenti remitti; & illam qua credit sibi remissa esse. Primum actum juxta ipsos, hominem disponere ad justificationem, secundum eum actu & reipsa justificare, tertium vero minime, sed per eum percipi jam factam justificationem, & inde fidelis animae solatium pendere. Quam subtilitatem quamquam non probemus, certum est iis tribui non posse, nisi per injuriam, & contra veritatem, quod doceant actum illum per quem justificamur, esse illum quo statuunt fideles singuli per Christum sibi remissa esse peccata, quandoquidem verbis expressis istud negant. Idque in illis ipsis tractatibus & quaestionibus, ubi eundem actum dicunt esse praecipuum & specificum fidei salvificae actum, & per eundem fidem justificantem definiunt. Nempe dicunt illum esse praecipuum actum fidei salvificae, quia praecipue facit ad pacem conscientiae, & fidelium consolationem; & specificum quoque, quia fidem salvificam ab historica discriminat: Et expressam ejus mentionem faciunt in fidei definitione, quia de tali fiducia & persuasione maxima erat mota controversia inter Scholam Romanam, & inter Reformatam.
pass_a_gloss: Indeed those very Doctors of the Reformed School on whose testimony that author chiefly relies — who accuses the Reformed of a corrupt Christian ethics so as to attribute to their whole School the opinion that the act of faith by which we are justified is certain trust concerning pardon of sins obtained from God — expressly and clearly deny that they think that; as has been abundantly proved above by the words and testimonies of Robert Baron, Rivet, Wendelin, Pareus, and Maresius. Baron, namely, distinguishes between trust of pardon to be obtained and trust of pardon obtained: both are for him a proper act of justifying faith; but the former precedes justification and is its instrument; the latter follows justification and is not its instrument. Rivet, Wendelin, Pareus, and Maresius distinguish still more subtly among trust by which someone believes sins are to be remitted to him, that by which he believes sins are being remitted to him in the present, and that by which he believes they have been remitted. The first act, according to them, disposes a person to justification; the second justifies him actually and in fact; the third not at all, but through it already-accomplished justification is perceived, and thence the believer's soul's comfort hangs. Which subtlety, though we do not approve it, it is certain cannot be attributed to them except by injury and against the truth that they teach the act by which we are justified to be that by which individual believers judge their sins remitted through Christ — since in express words they deny that. And that in those very treatises and questions where they call the same act the chief and specific act of saving faith and define justifying faith by it. Namely they call it the chief act of saving faith because it chiefly makes for peace of conscience and believers' consolation; and specific also because it discriminates saving from historical faith: and they make express mention of it in faith's definition because the greatest controversy between the Roman and Reformed Schools was moved concerning such trust and persuasion.
pass_b_english: Even the doctors the opponent cites — Baron, Rivet, Wendelin, Pareus, Maresius — expressly deny that trust in already remitted sins is the act by which we are justified.
Baron: trust of pardon still to be obtained instruments justification; trust of pardon already obtained follows it.

Rivet and company distinguish three tenses (sins to be remitted, now being remitted, already remitted) and make only the present tense formally justifying — a subtlety Le Blanc rejects, yet it still refutes pinning past remission persuasion on them as the justifying act.
They may call assurance chief or specific for consolation and to discriminate saving from historical faith, and because Rome contested it — not because it instruments justification.
